questions.q: Why do real web3 repos validate environment variables with a schema library (like zod) instead of using process.env directly?
options: process.env values are typed string | undefined, so trusting them directly means a missing variable surfaces as a confusing error deep inside the app instead of a clear one at startup
process.env cannot be read at all in TypeScript
Schema validation makes RPC calls faster
TypeScript requires all environment variables to be validated by law of the compiler
questions.explain: process.env.X is always typed string | undefined; parsing it through a schema at startup turns a missing/malformed variable into an immediate, clear failure instead of a confusing bug far from the real cause.

questions.q: What does the `satisfies` operator do that a plain type annotation (`const x: T = {...}`) does not?
options: It converts the object into a bigint
It checks the object against the type while keeping each property's exact literal type, instead of widening values to their general type
It disables type-checking entirely for that object
It is only usable on arrays, never objects
questions.explain: A plain annotation widens literal values (e.g. id: 1 becomes id: number); satisfies checks against the type but keeps the literal value (id: 1 stays the literal 1).

questions.q: In the generic `withRetry<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>)` wrapper, what does the type parameter `T` accomplish?
options: It forces every call to withRetry to return a string
It limits withRetry to only work with bigint-returning functions
It lets withRetry return whatever type `fn` returns, so the retry logic works for any async call without losing type information
It has no effect — T is purely decorative
questions.explain: Because T is generic, withRetry adapts to whatever fn returns (e.g. Promise<bigint>), giving callers full type safety without writing a separate retry function per return type.

questions.q: Why is `type SupportedChainId = 1 | 137 | 42161` safer than typing a chain ID as plain `number`?
options: Union types execute faster at runtime than number
number cannot represent chain IDs larger than 255
SupportedChainId automatically fetches the RPC URL for any chain
Passing an unsupported or typo'd chain ID to a function expecting SupportedChainId fails to compile, instead of failing later inside a function that assumed every chain was configured
questions.explain: A union of exact supported IDs means an unsupported chain ID is caught at the call site as a compile error, rather than causing a runtime failure deep inside code that assumed it was valid.

questions.q: What is a concrete downside of using `as const` alone (without `satisfies`) on a config object you also want checked against an interface?
options: as const converts every value to a string
as const locks the literal type but does not check the object's shape against any interface, so a typo'd key or wrong value type would not be caught
as const cannot be used on objects, only arrays
as const makes the object mutable at runtime
questions.explain: as const only narrows literal types — it doesn't validate the object's shape against an interface the way satisfies (or a type annotation) does, so structural mistakes can slip through.
